meta.title: Who really said "Fantasy is an exercise bicycle for the mind. It might not take you anywhere, but it tones up the muscles that can"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Pratchett's 1993 speech "Let There Be Dragons" has the image in different words. The popular one-liner is a later condensation of it.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Fantasy is an exercise bicycle for the mind. It might not take you anywhere, but it tones up the muscles that can'?
meta.ogDescription: The idea is Terry Pratchett's, from his 1993 speech "Let There Be Dragons". The tidy "Fantasy is…" wording is a later condensation.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: The image is Pratchett’s own. His 1993 speech “Let There Be Dragons” says the science fiction he read as a boy was “like an exercise bicycle for the mind — it doesn’t take you anywhere, but it certainly tones up the muscles.” The popular wording, “Fantasy is… the muscles that can”, is a later condensation, and we found no published Pratchett text that uses it.

source.heading: Where the words actually come from

docMeta.dd: Speech to the Booksellers Association Conference dinner, Torquay

source.excerpt: As a suddenly thirsting reader I escaped first of all to what was then called Outer Space. I read a lot of science fiction, which as I have said is only a 20th century subset of fantasy. And a lot of it was, in strict literary terms, rubbish. But this was good rubbish. It was like an exercise bicycle for the mind — it doesn’t take you anywhere, but it certainly tones up the muscles.
trail: 1993: Pratchett gave a speech, “Let There Be Dragons”, at the Booksellers Association Conference dinner in Torquay, and The Bookseller printed it on 11 June 1993. In it he says of the science fiction he read as a boy: “It was like an exercise bicycle for the mind — it doesn’t take you anywhere, but it certainly tones up the muscles” (reprint in Science Fiction Chronicle, Oct. 1993 ↗).

2000: The condensed wording is printed under Pratchett’s name in the Chicon 2000 Worldcon program book ↗: “Fantasy is an exercise bicycle for the mind. It might not take you anywhere, but it tones up the muscles that can. Of course, I could be wrong.”
2014: The speech appears in Pratchett’s nonfiction collection A Slip of the Keyboard ↗, listed as “Let There Be Dragons (1993)”.
Today: Wikiquote’s talk page lists the popular wording under “Unsourced” (Talk:Terry Pratchett ↗). We found no Quote Investigator article on the line.
source.excerptNote: This is the text as reprinted, with permission from The Bookseller, in Science Fiction Chronicle (October 1993), which calls it an edited version of the speech. Pratchett is talking about science fiction, which he calls a subset of fantasy, and he says “certainly tones up the muscles”, not “tones up the muscles that can”.

source.rightsNote: The words come from Pratchett’s speech “Let There Be Dragons”, first printed in The Bookseller in 1993. That is well after 1931, and the 1993 reprint carries a “Copyright © 1993 by Terry Pratchett” notice, so the text is in copyright in the US. The popular one-liner is a condensation of that copyrighted passage, not a public-domain saying.

author.name: Terry Pratchett
author.heading: About Terry Pratchett
author.metaLine: 1948–2015 · English fantasy novelist, creator of Discworld
author.bio: Sir Terry Pratchett (28 April 1948 – 12 March 2015) wrote the Discworld series of 41 comic fantasy novels. By Wikipedia’s count he sold more than 100 million books in 43 languages. He was knighted for services to literature in the 2009 New Year Honours, and he often spoke up for fantasy and for children’s reading.

misattribution.heading: What the popular version gets wrong
misattribution.intro: The thought is genuinely Pratchett’s. The polished wording that circulates is not what his 1993 text says.

items.who: “Fantasy is an exercise bicycle for the mind… tones up the muscles that can”
items.why: In the 1993 speech the comparison is about the science fiction he read as a boy, “good rubbish”, and it ends “it certainly tones up the muscles.” It does not say “Fantasy is”, “might not take you anywhere” or “the muscles that can” (1993 reprint ↗).

This closing line often travels with the quote. It is printed with the condensed wording in the Chicon 2000 program book ↗, but it is not in the speech as reprinted in Science Fiction Chronicle. We could not tell who first wrote the condensed form.
The one-liner is usually given with no source at all. Wikiquote’s talk page files it under “Unsourced” (Talk:Terry Pratchett ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The exercise-bicycle image comes from Pratchett’s own 1993 speech “Let There Be Dragons”: “It was like an exercise bicycle for the mind — it doesn’t take you anywhere, but it certainly tones up the muscles” (read it ↗). Credit him for the idea, and quote the 1993 wording if you need his exact words.

context.heading: Why he said it
lead: “Let There Be Dragons” was Pratchett’s speech to booksellers in defense of fantasy as children’s reading. He starts with the first book he read for pleasure, The Wind in the Willows, and then turns on the old charge that fantasy is mere escapism. In the same passage as the exercise bicycle he says, “There is nothing wrong with escapism. The key points of consideration, though, are what you are escaping from, and where you are escaping to.”

So the exercise bicycle was his answer to the claim that genre reading is a waste of time. It may lead nowhere in itself, but it builds the mental strength that does take you places. The condensed version keeps that point. It just isn’t his wording.
context.detailsSummary: Did he ever say it the popular way?
detailsBody: Pratchett used the image more than once. He is one of the writers interviewed in Leonard S. Marcus’s The Wand in the Word: Conversations with Writers of Fantasy (Candlewick, 2006) ↗. A full-text search of the Internet Archive’s scan of that book shows him saying “Fantasy is like an exercise bicycle for the mind. It might not actually take…”, which is close to the popular wording. The scan is borrow-only, so we could not read the full sentence.
The exact circulating sentence, with “tones up the muscles that can” and “Of course, I could be wrong”, is in print under his name by 2000. We have not found it in any published Pratchett text.
context.pull: There is nothing wrong with escapism.
